title: The Factors that Affect Learning: Five Ways in Which Evidence Can Help Learning Happen
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Opening his series on factors that affect learning, Skelton argues that anyone interested in learning must be interested in evidence, because evidence is how we know whether getting better has happened. He notes that knowledge is mainly assessed, understanding mainly evaluated and skills both, so the issue is appropriateness rather than importance. He then lists five ways evidence helps: it compares then with now, it diagnoses who has not improved and why, it supports feedback for students and families, it focuses minds on what matters, and it allows comparisons between classes, schools and systems. A conversation with a teacher who equated a lively lesson with learning, and a middle school that traced a maths decline back to one primary year group, make the points concrete. He ends with a five-question checklist and promises that the next post covers how evidence can obstruct learning.
points: Learning-focused evidence always compares then and now, so enthusiasm or a bright pupil's questions are not evidence of learning.
Good evidence diagnoses who has not improved and why, giving the teacher what is needed to plan the next step.
Feedback grounded in evidence lets students and parents act on it, and skills learning in particular benefits from rubrics describing Beginning, Developing and Mastering.
Measuring what matters shapes what people value, so the bike-riding example (balance, steering, braking) shows the benefit of limiting evidence to the few things that count.
The middle school maths case shows comparison across schools and year groups finding a breakdown point that internal guesswork missed.
quotes: Anyone who says they are driven by or interested in learning has to be interested in evidence. Anyone who says that they aren’t interested in evidence isn’t really interested in learning.

Learning-focused evidence is that which allows us to answer the most important question of all: ‘How do you know whether learning has happened?’ If getting better is at the heart of learning, then evidence is the way we know whether getting better is happening.
Both assessment and evaluation matter equally, just as the acquisition of knowledge and the deepening of understanding both matter. The issue is not one of importance. It is one of appropriateness.

But put simply, my colleague, whom I came to know as a committed teacher and a lovely, kind man, didn’t actually have much evidence of anything to do with learning from his lesson. He did have some evidence about other things.

Evidence doesn’t just answer the question ‘Have they got better?’. It provides the fuel to answer the questions ’Who hasn’t got better, why haven’t they and what can we do to help them.’ In this central task of teaching and helping children and students get better, without evidence we are simply hamstrung.

Without good, evidence-based feedback, learners can’t begin to self-improve. Getting feedback - providing it is focused around the three questions that ended the previous small section - gives clues to a learner about what to do to get better.
We are told to measure what matters. But what matters to people is what we measure.
